Huynh T.lab_name: Zoghbi Lab, Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Huynh T.role: Research associate at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and co-author on a long run of papers from Andrea Ballabio's group on TFEB, the master switch for lysosome and autophagy genes, including the work that tied TFEB to mTOR, starvation and fat metabolism
Huynh T.sub: Research Associate, Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine (Zoghbi Lab) · co-author with the Ballabio, Settembre and Sardiello groups (2011–2026)
story: Cells keep themselves clean with lysosomes, small acid-filled bags that break down worn-out parts, and with autophagy, the process that delivers those parts to the lysosome. In 2011 Carmine Settembre, Andrea Ballabio and colleagues, with Tuong Huynh among the co-authors, showed that one transcription factor, TFEB, switches on a whole programme of autophagy and lysosome genes when cells are starved (SET2011). In that first paper TFEB was controlled by the kinase ERK2. The 2012 follow-up (SET2012) found the link to mTORC1, the growth-control complex that sits on the lysosome surface: when nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB and keeps it out of the nucleus, so the lysosome itself reports its state to the genes that build it.

The 2013 paper (SET2013) moved into living mice. Fasting switched on the TFEB gene in liver, muscle and kidney, and TFEB then boosted its own production in a feed-forward loop. In the liver it drove fat breakdown largely through PGC-1alpha and PPARalpha, and extra liver TFEB protected mice from diet-induced obesity. The most recent paper (FER2026) used kidney-specific mouse models to separate mTORC1 activity from TFEB/TFE3 activity and found that overactive mTORC1, not TFEB/TFE3 alone, is the main driver of kidney cysts and tumours in models of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.

PubMed lists Tuong Huynh on about a dozen TFEB, lysosome and autophagy papers with the Ballabio, Settembre or Sardiello groups between 2011 and 2026. The early papers give no affiliation for this author; a 2020 paper and the 2026 kidney paper place Huynh at the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, and the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute of Texas Children's Hospital in Houston, where Ballabio's US laboratory is based. The Baylor College of Medicine staff directory lists Tuong B. Huynh as a Research Associate in the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, attached to the Zoghbi Lab.
sources: PubMed search: Huynh T[Author] AND TFEB/lysosomal/autophagy AND Ballabio/Sardiello/Settembre (13 records, 2011-2026)
Huynh T.note: Baylor directory (Tuong B. Huynh, Research Associate, Mol. & Human Gen.) attaches the person to the Zoghbi Lab, not the Ballabio lab; same name, institution and department as the 2020/2026 PubMed affiliation, so accepted. Middle initial B appears only on the directory. No education listed, no ORCID.

Glass DJ.role: Muscle biologist and Regeneron vice president for ageing research, member of the US National Academy of Sciences, who helped discover the muscle-wasting enzymes MuRF1 and MAFbx and co-authored the first trials of low-dose mTOR inhibition in older people
Glass DJ.sub: Vice President, Aging/Age-Related Disorders, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (since 2019) · Senior Lecturer in Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School · head of the musculoskeletal programme, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research · Regeneron (about 15 years, earlier) · postdoc with Charles Cantor and Stephen Goff, Columbia University · MD, New York Medical College
story: David Glass is a co-author of two Atlas trials from the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research that asked whether a short course of a low-dose mTOR inhibitor can help the ageing immune system. In MAN2014, older volunteers took everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin-like drug, for six weeks before a flu shot, and their antibody response to the vaccine rose by about 20 percent; fewer of their T cells carried PD-1, a marker of exhausted immune cells. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of everolimus and BEZ235 (a drug that blocks PI3K and mTOR at the active site) was linked to fewer reported infections over the following year.

These trials are the main human basis for the idea of weekly low-dose rapalogs as an anti-ageing intervention. Their limits matter: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not proof of fewer infections, and a later phase 3 trial of BEZ235 (RTB101) alone did not confirm a clinical benefit.

Glass trained as a physician, with an MD from New York Medical College, and chose research over further clinical training. Postdoctoral work followed with Charles Cantor and then Stephen Goff at Columbia University. During about 15 years at Regeneron, Glass began studying skeletal muscle and helped identify MuRF1 and MAFbx, two muscle-specific enzymes that tag proteins for destruction when muscle wastes away (MAFbx was found independently by Alfred Goldberg's group, who named it atrogin-1). The lab later showed that myosin heavy chain, the main motor protein of muscle, is a key target of MuRF1, and that the kinase Akt drives muscle growth and links growth and wasting through the FOXO proteins.

At Novartis, Glass led the musculoskeletal research programme, working on myostatin, GDF-11 and activin A and leading development of the antibody bimagrumab. As senior author there, Glass led a 2019 study in aged rats showing that partial inhibition of mTORC1 with a rapalog counteracted the age-related loss of muscle mass. In 2019 Glass returned to Regeneron as Vice President of Aging/Age-Related Disorders and also holds a post as Senior Lecturer in Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School. Recent papers cover how common low muscle mass is among people with obesity in the USA, a 2025 trial identifying GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A as the main brakes on muscle mass in postmenopausal women, and, in 2026, why keeping muscle matters during drug-induced weight loss. In April 2024 Glass was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences.
Glass DJ.note: Career facts from the 2024 PNAS/PMC piece on Glass's NAS election (PMC11232304). It confirms Glass discovered MuRF1/MAFbx at Regeneron, so the two 2001 Atlas muscle papers listing 'D J Glass' at Regeneron are very likely the same person and could be linked to this profile. No ORCID seen. The HDAC4 sentence from the old story was dropped to keep the paragraph short; restore if wanted.

Cybulski N.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Cybulski N.role: Cell biologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue helps control how big the whole body grows
Cybulski N.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2008–2014, most recent confirmed affiliation) · PhD, University of Basel (2010, with Michael N. Hall) · later address in Montreal, Canada (2014) · current position not confirmed
story: Nadine Cybulski is a co-author of two Atlas mouse studies from Michael Hall's lab. In 2008, mice lacking raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue stayed lean, resisted diet-induced obesity and burned more energy in their fat. In 2012, mice lacking rictor, the core of mTORC2, only in the liver could not switch the liver to its fed-state programme, so it kept making glucose and made less fat. Both are mouse results.

Cybulski did a PhD in Hall's lab at the Biozentrum. The thesis, "New insights into the 'in vivo' and 'in vitro' functions of mammalian TOR complex 2", was accepted by the University of Basel in 2010, supervised by Hall with Markus Ruegg as co-referee. Cybulski's main paper, as first author in PNAS in 2009, removed rictor from fat tissue. The mice grew larger overall, with bigger organs such as heart, kidney and bone. The mice had high insulin and raised levels of the growth factor IGF1 and its partner protein IGFBP3. The study showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue acts as a brake on growth of the whole body. With Hall, Cybulski also wrote a 2009 review, "TOR complex 2: a signaling pathway of its own", and described mouse cells in which raptor or rictor can be switched off on demand, a tool used by many labs.

Cybulski also co-authored studies with Oded Meyuhas's group in Jerusalem on how mTOR controls translation of a class of messenger RNAs called TOP mRNAs. A 2014 paper gives a later address in Montreal, Canada. A current position could not be confirmed.
Cybulski N.note: PubMed also lists a Nicolas Cybulski (plant biology, Ghent) under Cybulski N; different person, excluded. The 2014 paper gives a present address in Montreal (organisation abbreviated ADAM); could not be resolved. PhD confirmed from the Basel edoc thesis record (thesis no. 9052, 2010). Pritchard KI.lab_name: Sunnybrook Odette Cancer Centre and Sunnybrook Research Institute, University of Toronto (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)
Pritchard KI.role: Breast cancer medical oncologist at Sunnybrook in Toronto, professor emerita at the University of Toronto and long-time leader of breast cancer trials, co-author of the BOLERO-2 everolimus trial
Pritchard KI.sub: Medical oncologist, Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre · Professor Emerita, Department of Medicine and Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, University of Toronto · chair, later co-chair, Breast Site Committee, Canadian Cancer Trials Group · founding member (1984) and co-chair (since 2000), Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group · Order of Canada (2017)
story: Kathleen Pritchard is a co-author of both main reports of BOLERO-2 in this Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had kept growing despite an aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy (BAS2012, PIC2014). All the women took the hormone drug exemestane; half also took everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Resistance to hormone therapy in these cancers is linked to overactive mTOR signalling, and adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review in the first report). That result led to the approval of everolimus for this use. The final report (PIC2014) confirmed the gain in progression-free survival, but overall survival was not significantly longer: median 31.0 versus 26.6 months. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis).

For the mTOR story the trial is a landmark: it was the first large test showing that blocking mTORC1 helps patients with a common cancer, and it also shows the limits, a delay in tumour growth without a clear gain in overall survival.

Pritchard is a medical oncologist at Sunnybrook in Toronto and professor emerita in the Department of Medicine and the Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation at the University of Toronto. She chaired and later co-chaired the breast cancer committee of the Canadian Cancer Trials Group and has guided many multi-centre breast cancer trials in Canada and abroad. She was a founding member in 1984, and since 2000 co-chair, of the Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group, which pools the raw data of randomised trials worldwide to measure how well breast cancer treatments work. PubMed lists close to 190 papers with her name and a Toronto affiliation, most of them on breast cancer trials and treatment outcomes, including the 2015 analysis of which tumour gene changes predicted benefit from everolimus in BOLERO-2. In 2017 she was appointed to the Order of Canada for her contributions to the treatment of breast cancer in women.

Thelen AM.lab_name: Greenberg Lab, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Thelen AM.role: Cell biologist who did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lysosome lab at UC Berkeley, first author of a 2017 review on the lysosome's roles in lipid metabolism, and later a postdoctoral scholar in Philip Greenberg's lab at Fred Hutch
Thelen AM.sub: Postdoctoral scholar, Philip Greenberg lab, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle (per Zoncu lab alumni page) · graduate student, Zoncu Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (about 2017–2019)
story: Ashley Thelen is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Together the two papers show how mTORC1 reads the state of the lysosome: what nutrients it holds, and whether the Rag switch on its surface is in the 'on' position. Both are cell and protein studies.

Thelen did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, which studies how the lysosome senses nutrients. There Thelen was first author of a 2017 Trends in Cell Biology review, written with Zoncu, on the emerging roles of the lysosome in lipid metabolism, and co-authored a 2019 Molecular Biology of the Cell paper from Schekman's lab at Berkeley on how an autophagy-specific PI3-kinase complex controls LC3 lipidation, an early step in building autophagosomes. The Zoncu lab's alumni list gives Thelen's next position as postdoctoral scholar in Philip Greenberg's lab at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle.
